appraisal_events.evidence: Rachel, now a celebrated actress, is to recite verses of Musset and La Fontaine at Mme Verdurin's matinee, and rumor in Paris holds that although invitations went out in the princesse's name, it is really Rachel who is receiving; she has also become the duchesse de Guermantes's intimate friend.
appraisal_events.explanation: Rachel undergoes a striking public rise: the former disdained actress now headlines and effectively hosts the era's most fashionable gathering and is intimate with the duchesse.

appraisal_events.evidence: The newer generations, seeing the duchesse befriend Rachel and neglect the Faubourg Saint-Germain, concluded she must be some déclassée who had never truly belonged to the top tier ('n'avait jamais été tout à fait du gratin').
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse's local reputation is undermined among younger observers by her visible intimacy with a former demimondaine, though the narrator leaves open whether this reveals genuine unconventional discernment or simple mediocrity.

appraisal_events.evidence: Nearly every guest invited to the dying Berma's tea abandons her to attend Rachel's recital at the Guermantes matinee instead; the gathering becomes 'a funeral meal,' Berma sits with death visibly on her face, and even the one guest who came keeps glancing at the clock before finally leaving too.
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage stages a stark public abandonment: society's collective preference for Rachel's party over Berma's leaves the great, dying tragedienne isolated and eclipsed in her final days.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mme Verdurin, now princesse de Guermantes by remarriage, is said to enjoy claiming a long-standing intimacy with Gilberte's mother and Saint-Loup's family 'to try to give her new elegance a past'; the narrator dryly notes that one easily arranges accounts of a past nobody else can verify.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator quietly exposes Mme Verdurin's claimed old intimacy with the Guermantes-adjacent families as a convenient, self-serving embellishment of her recently acquired grand position.

status_effects.explanation: Rachel's public performance at, and rumored real hosting of, the most fashionable gathering in Paris marks a clear and visible rise in standing.
Her reputation among the rising generation suffers because her intimacy with Rachel is read as proof she was never truly first-rank, even though the narrator leaves the underlying judgment unsettled.
Berma is left suffering and visibly dying while nearly everyone she counted on deserts her for a rival gathering.
The boundary between the desirable gathering and Berma's own is shown starkly: guests cross over to the Guermantes matinee en masse, leaving Berma's table nearly empty.
The narrator's ironic aside about conveniently arranged accounts of an unverifiable past locally undercuts Mme Verdurin's self-presentation.

ambiguities: The narrator offers two competing, unresolved explanations for the duchesse de Guermantes's new intimacy with Rachel -- hidden anti-snobbish discernment versus genuine intellectual mediocrity and boredom -- leaving the exact character of her local diminishment uncertain.

Bare mentions of 'la princesse de Guermantes' in this passage are resolved to Mme Verdurin based on the passage's own internal clarification (Gilberte's uncle's mesalliance in marrying Mme Verdurin), consistent with the reference sheet noting this title later passed to her by remarriage.
